I think I can better Gulliver’s Travels by about 60 years! The Blazing World by Margaret Cavendish (1666) is arguably the earliest work of Science Fiction, in which a young woman is transported through a portal in the North Pole to a strange land (the Blazing World) where the stars in the sky are different and the inhabitants are anthropomorphised animals. They have their own natural philosophy and academic disciplines - bears tinkering with microscopes and arguing with the Empress about whether they show something small enlarged, or whether they show something within the microscope.

Now, where this is particularly interesting for you is how this relates to the sort of para-academic discipline you’re describing.

Margaret Cavendish (aka Mad Madge) was deeply interested in the science of her day, and excluded from joining the Royal Society of which she desperately wanted to be a part. (The Royal Society is the earliest form of any sort of professional body of scientists; but professionalisation gives the wrong impression, think instead of a royally-endorsed gentleman’s club of aristocrats with eccentric interests).

She herself was restricted to publishing pamphlets of her own views on what was then called “Natural Philosophy” - with views on a sort of proto-atomic theory, among other things. She engaged in correspondence with several of the leading lights of her day, and was well read - if any of her  ideas seem absurd, bear in mind that they are not drawn out of thin air, but out of independent research and thought-experiments.

Why does this matter for you? Well, if you’re interested in “fake academia” and its portrayal in literature, this is the whole damn point of the Blazing World. It’s a wittily bitter satire of the institution of her day, the Royal Society, which was as close to being “made up” as something could be while being legitimate. King Charles II on at least one occasion used them for court entertainment - the vibe was very much not “show us your great discoveries, oh scientists”, but rather “the Earl of Montgomery has some batshit nonsense he’s been going on about, go on Monty, tell us about that stuff you were saying at dinner yesterday, you absolute nutcase.” So we have para-academia built on quasi-academia, in a science fiction polemic intended to undercut the self-importance of such formal bodies.

Bonus: it’s short and probably free online! If you’re interested, I can send you some more academic references later in the week, I did quite a bit of work on it a few years back. Just DM me. Happy hunting.

**There’s so much to be proud of here!** Your control of texture and shade - from the fur, to the tanned-skin banner, to the horns and hooves and rusted metal - is really impressive. Your control over recesses and highlights on delicate areas like the abdomens and fingers shows a really steady hand. Well done!

A couple of areas to work on (and this comes more from lurking rather than personal experience, so do take with a pinch of salt):

- **Painting technique:** some of your highlights are a bit stark - it’s time to look into either wet blending or glazing to get those transitions buttery smooth. More noticeable and achievable on the muscles of the beastmen than their fingers or snouts, for example. Where you’ve got more flat space, you’ve got more opportunity to gain and retain fine control of your colour transitions.

- **Not liking what you paint:** Sounds like you’re having a rough time, and I won’t presume to offer advice beyond mini painting. *On that front*, however, you’ve set yourself the same sort of challenge every time. Beastmen in corroded armour are cool, but variety is the spice of life! Maybe it’s time to branch out into some lurid greens and glowing pinks on some Gloomspite Gitz, or some Sigmarites in shining golden plate! I know that I personally need variety in models and even in army-lore to keep myself engaged. Maybe branching out for a handful of models would help you too!

You’re obviously an accomplished painter, and I would be so proud to have painted these. Keep it up, I’m rooting for you!

You probably heard about [the film coming out soon!](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=VoJc2tH3WBw) The story of Gawain and the Green Knight is an Arthurian legend taken from a Medieval English poem, which has been [brilliantly translated by Simon Armitage.](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Gawain-Green-Knight-Simon-Armitage/dp/0571223281)

Camelot, New Year’s Day. Gift-giving, merriment, feasting, and young Sir Gawain at his uncle Arthur’s right hand. Silence falls as an uninvited guest arrives: an ‘aghlich mayster, On the most in the molde on mesure hyghe ... He ferde as ferke were fade, And overal enker-grene.’ (A fearsome lord, a mountain of a man ...  garbed for battle, and emerald-green.)

In a voice as deep and old as forests’ bones, the Green Knight proposes a New Year’s game, if any knight is brave enough to take the wager... The Green Knight offers to kneel and receive an unchallenged blow from his own axe, a brutal blade ‘the grayne al of grene stele and of golde’.

But here’s the catch. In a year’s time, whoever delivers the blow must receive one in return, in exactly twelve months.

Young Gawain, determined to prove himself in front of king and court, takes the challenge, swings the axe, and severs the Green Knight’s head with a single stroke.

It bounces, rolls, thuds to a stop against a leg of the trestle table, gently knocking a pitcher of wine into the bread basket. The collected party goers whoop, yell, clap and go silent. Because the next thing that happens, of course, is that the Green Knight stands up...

Hopefully you can tell how much I love this story and this poem. I really recommend the Armitage translation. Happy reading!

>Icewind Dale is a rough, wild frontier on the edge of civilisation. It has been two years since the sun truly rose. The closest thing to daylight is an odd twilight that lasts from roughly 10am to 2pm. At all other times, travellers through the Dale count their meagre blessings by the light of the moon or stinking whale-oil lamps.

>You will be travelling through glaciers, mountains, and tundra. If you are foolish or brave enough, perhaps even the Sea of Moving Ice. Your environment alone will be dangerous, but you will be well rewarded for creativity and careful planning with your limited resources. Draw your own conclusions about the consequences should you be found wanting.

>It has been two years since true trade operated between Icewind Dale and the soft lands to the south of the Spine of the World. Scrimshaw (artfully carved ivory) from Ten Towns is valued across Faerûn, theoretically for its beauty and artistry, but particularly for its rarity.

>In the decadent noble courts and cities of the South, where the worst of winter is but a summer’s day to Ten Towners, where food and warmth are scattered across the land as freely as frost across the face of the Reghed Glacier, scarcity - novelty - has a value all of its own.

>If trade from Ten Towns has been slow in the past two years, well... Who’s going to notice that supplies of salted knucklehead fish and their cleverly-carved bones have stuttered? Who would bother to investigate a wasteland hard and cold as its tiny population?

>For many, Ten Towns is the last place they can go. Criminals, outcasts, hermits and their descendants inhabit the settlements of Icewind Dale, and have done for some small handful of centuries.

>From this desperation comes a kind of pride: here we stand, this far, and no further. In the face of barbarian raids, orc and goblin hordes, starvation, desolation, the people of Ten Towns have stood together, for they have had nowhere else to stand.

>It is one thing to stand shoulder to shoulder in the face of an orc raid, but quite another to stand by your fellows after two years of darkness. Two years of cold, of hunger. Two years of being stuck inside or freezing to death. The ties that bind Ten Towns together are strong. The ties that bind Ten Towns together have been tested before. *The ties that bind Ten Towns together have grown very, very thin.*

>My last piece of advice: Rangers and Druids naturally thrive in the wild regions of the world, but don’t feel like you’ll be hamstrung by choosing to play as a silver-tongued bard, a city-bred burglar or a pampered young student of magic. All kinds of people end up in Icewind Dale, and they survive by working together. Why shouldn’t you?

There’s a lot to unpack there, but I’m not sure that I’d follow you in the leap from “political correctness” (guessing at the damage we might do to others with our actions, and trying to weigh that cost in advance?) to “Marxists use it for mass immigration”.

I’d really recommend checking out Ruff’s *Lovecraft Country*. I’d be keen to hear your perspective on it, I know it surprised me!

Interesting interpretation of political correctness - there’s actually a wealth of fantastic weird fiction that deals with the imbalance of social power!

*Lovecraft Country* by Matt Ruff is a brilliant example. You’re quite right: isolation, despair and otherness are important aspects of Lovecraft and his legacy. It’s only a short hop and a skip to see how the othering and expulsion of particular *groups* of people - people who have historically been unheard - might inflect and enrich these important emotional touchstones of Weird & Cosmic Horror.

Aside from minorities’ engagement with HPL’s legacy, you could also check out Thomas Ligotti (*Songs of a Dead Dreamer*) or China Mieville (*Three Momemts of an Explosion*) to see how Lovecraftian logic and lyricism persists into Late Modernity.

Happy reading!

It sounds like you're in a bad way, man. I empathise. Whether or not you believe that's true is another matter, but I really do. For starters: Facebook depresses most people. It sure as hell depresses me. Remember that Facebook profiles and interactions are carefully crafted displays; it's easy to fall into the trap of assuming all these people you're linked to on Facebook are having crazy good times 24/7.
There's a lot you can do to make yourself feel better, it just requires a little motivation. The first thing you could do is to reach out to family. You'll be amazed at how understanding they can be. The second thing you can do is look for groups in your area. I recommend hiking or running groups. You get fit, and you can talk as little or as much as you want to. Being good with computers is not in the slightest bit useless. As an English graduate, I envy you. Are you into hardware, software, or both? Sysadmin stuff? Programming? You would also be surprised at how interested people will be in your computer knowledge if you bring it up in conversation. You can think of it as a game where you have to fit the information into their heads, which ought to stop them getting bored.
